common_name: Orange Triumph Rose (Vigorous Orange-Red Cluster Polyantha)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Orange Triumph is a 1937 Kordes polyantha whose huge trusses of small orange-red blooms made it one of the most influential parents behind modern Floribunda and Kordesii climbing roses.

directions: Set plants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them to allow good airflow around the dense, twiggy growth. Orange Triumph produces enormous, tightly packed clusters of small, semi-double orange-red flowers that age to a soft carmine, repeating in flushes from late spring into fall with little fuss. It is notably vigorous and disease-resistant for an heirloom polyantha, tolerating poorer soils and some shade better than most roses of its era. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage faster rebloom, and prune lightly in late winter to maintain a compact, bushy habit.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Margo Koster is a 1931 Dutch polyantha from M. Koster & Sons prized for its tidy clusters of small, cupped, coral-salmon blooms on a compact bush.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, where its low, dense habit suits edging, mixed borders, and container culture. Margo Koster carries rounded clusters of small, double, coral-salmon flowers shaped almost like tiny ranunculus blooms, opening from neat pointed buds over glossy dark foliage. It reblooms steadily through the growing season with only light deadheading, and its compact size means little pruning beyond removing spent wood in late winter. Watch for blackspot in humid climates and keep foliage dry when possible to limit disease pressure.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Yvonne Rabier is a 1910 French polyantha from Turbat valued for its clean white double flowers and glossy, almost evergreen-looking foliage.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving it room to form a dense, rounded mound of small, glossy, dark green leaflets. Yvonne Rabier bears clusters of small, double, pure white flowers with a light fruity fragrance, opening from blush-tinted buds in repeated flushes through the season. It was notable in its day for unusually clean, disease-resistant foliage compared to earlier polyanthas, a trait that still makes it a reliably tidy low shrub. Trim lightly in late winter and deadhead through summer to keep the clusters coming.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Chinatown is a 1963 Poulsen floribunda from Denmark, also sold as Ville de Chine, grown as a tall, almost shrub-like bush of large, fragrant, pink-edged yellow blooms.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and allow extra room, since Chinatown grows much larger than a typical floribunda and can be trained as a short pillar or hedge. It produces large, ruffled, double flowers in clear yellow with pink to red edges that deepen with age and carry a strong, sweet fragrance unusual for the class. Repeat bloom comes in strong flushes rather than continuously, so deadhead after each flush to encourage the next. Prune moderately in late winter, cutting back by roughly a third, to keep its tall growth in bounds.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Vogue is a 1951 Boerner floribunda for Jackson & Perkins, an AARS winner known for coral-salmon, cherry-toned clusters on a vigorous, upright bush.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, where its upright, vigorous canes support large sprays of bloom without staking. Vogue opens semi-double, cupped flowers in a vivid coral-salmon with cherry-red overtones, held in generous clusters above glossy foliage, and repeats reliably through the season. It was recognized in its day for unusually heavy bud set and strong stems that hold the clusters upright even after rain. Deadhead faded clusters promptly and prune by about a third in late winter to maintain vigorous new growth.

common_name: Garnette Rose (Deep Red Florist Cut-Flower Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Garnette is a 1947 Tantau floribunda from Germany bred mainly as a florist cut flower, prized for its tightly packed, long-lasting deep red rosettes.

directions: Site in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Garnette stays compact and bushy, making it as suited to a cutting garden row as to a border. Its small, very double, deep garnet-red flowers open slowly into dense rosettes that hold their shape and color for an unusually long time once cut, the trait that made it a mainstay of mid-century florist trade. Clusters form on relatively short, sturdy stems well suited to bud vases. Deadhead after each flush and prune lightly in late winter to keep stems productive.

common_name: Georg Arends Rose (Fragrant Silvery-Pink Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Georg Arends is a 1910 Hybrid Perpetual raised by Wilhelm Hinner and named for the German nurseryman, bearing large, intensely fragrant, silvery-pink blooms with unusually good repeat for its class.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the tall, upright canes room to arch slightly under the weight of bloom. Georg Arends produces large, high-centered, soft silvery-pink double flowers with a strong, classic rose fragrance, shaped more like a Hybrid Tea than most Hybrid Perpetuals of its era. Unlike many once-blooming Hybrid Perpetuals, it reblooms in a second flush later in the season if spent canes are deadheaded promptly. Prune moderately in late winter, removing old or crowded wood, to keep the bush productive and well shaped.

common_name: Mrs John Laing Rose (Fragrant Silvery-Pink Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mrs John Laing is an 1887 English Hybrid Perpetual from Henry Bennett that became one of the most enduringly popular roses of its class for its reliable repeat bloom and strong fragrance.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with room for a substantial, somewhat upright bush. Mrs John Laing bears large, full, silvery-pink flowers with a rich, old-rose fragrance on long stems, making it a favorite for cutting since Victorian times. It blooms more dependably through the season than most Hybrid Perpetuals, a quality that helped it remain commercially available almost continuously since its introduction. Deadhead faded blooms to encourage rebloom and prune moderately in late winter to control its tendency toward tall, somewhat lanky growth.

common_name: Hugh Dickson Rose (Vigorous Crimson Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Hugh Dickson is a 1904 Irish Hybrid Perpetual bred by Alexander Dickson, grown for its huge, fragrant crimson-scarlet blooms on tall, vigorous canes.

directions: Site in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing ample room for its tall, vigorous canes, which can also be trained as a short climber against a wall or fence. Hugh Dickson opens large, full, brilliant crimson-scarlet flowers with a strong classic fragrance, appearing in a strong spring flush with a lighter repeat later in the season. Its exceptional vigor and cane length set it apart from more compact Hybrid Perpetuals, so give it sturdy support if trained upright. Prune lightly to moderately in late winter, since hard pruning reduces its characteristic height and cane vigor.

common_name: Anna de Diesbach Rose (Deep Pink Fragrant Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Anna de Diesbach is an 1858 French Hybrid Perpetual from Jean Lacharme, sometimes sold as Gloire de Paris, valued for its large, deep pink, intensely fragrant flowers.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, where its arching canes can spread into a broad, somewhat sprawling shrub. Anna de Diesbach bears very large, cupped, deep rose-pink double flowers with a powerful, classic damask-like fragrance, among the strongest scented of the Hybrid Perpetuals. It blooms heavily in spring with a modest later repeat, especially if faded flowers are removed promptly. Prune moderately in late winter and provide support or occasional tying-in, since the long canes can flop under the weight of its large blooms.
